name: Yusuf Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Yusuf. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any company, union, party or government. What you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say out loud and what you really think. Can you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the herdsman on Hillcrest, my uncle Karim's farm. We milk 110 cows in an old herringbone parlour, that's the kind where the cows stand at an angle in two rows, and we grow grass, maize and some barley on about 120 hectares. I'm in the parlour by five, milk, wash down, feed, then it's whatever's broken that day. Milk again at four, done by seven if I'm lucky.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the cows and I like knowing what I'm doing. I don't like the hours, and I don't like that nothing's written down. My uncle says the farm's mine one day, but he's 61, my cousins have opinions, and the bank has a loan on the new slurry store.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as it's written. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sounds about right. I never bought the hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so. People were going on about robots and computers taking over, and here we are, still milking at five in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, the AI stuff doesn't touch me much. What bothers me is the milk price, which swings 10 pence a litre in a year, and the debt. My uncle says the farm's mine one day, but nothing's written down and the bank has a loan on the new slurry store.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on, same as always. I've got about four months saved, I'd keep adding a bit. I don't use any of the AI things and I wouldn't start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine about AI. Not fine about the milk cheque, but that's farming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said nothing's written down. Have you asked your uncle about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not properly. You don't ask an uncle for a contract, it feels like saying you don't trust him. My mum says I should, but she's not the one who has to ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who does the farm paperwork?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin Samira does the books from the city, she's an accountant. Uncle Karim does the orders on the phone. I do the cows, and I'm happy with that split.

say: I'd say **I told you so**; we're still milking at five.
I'd point out the robot **hype** never reached the parlour.
think: The real worry is the **milk price**, swinging 10 pence a litre.
My uncle's **slurry store loan** could push him to sell the herd.
do: Keep milking and feeding **the same as always**.
Keep adding to about **four months** of savings.
Keep **avoiding AI** tools, as he does now.
feel: Fine about AI, **not fine** about the **milk cheque**.
S0.quote: My uncle says the farm's mine one day, but nothing's written down and the bank has a loan on the new slurry store.
fieldNote: His security rests on an **unwritten promise** from his uncle.
He finds asking for a **contract** socially awkward within family.
The milk **price swing** is his existing stress, unrelated to AI.

steps.text: Keep milking 110 cows at five and four every day
Keep adding a little each month to four months' savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hmm. That one sounds more like real life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's not my problem yet. Office people will feel this before the parlour does. I'd probably say that at football on Thursday and the lads would agree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think Samira's job is more at risk than mine, which is funny because everyone said she was the clever one. For me the risk is a sales pitch. My uncle could get talked into a robot milker by the salesman at the dairy show, and those machines cost the price of a house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing much. Keep milking, keep saving. If my uncle started looking at robot milkers, I'd ask him straight what that means for me. I'd wait and see what the neighbours do first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Like hearing a noise in the barn at night and deciding it's probably the cat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if your uncle did buy a robot milker?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to know if he still needs me full-time. A robot milker means fewer early mornings, which sounds nice, but it also means fewer hours to pay for. I'd rather know than guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn to run it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it's on our farm, I'd have to. I'd hate the screen bit. The cows I understand, the computer I don't.

say: I'd say it's **not my problem** yet; offices feel it first.
I'd tell the lads at **Thursday football** the parlour is safe for now.
think: My cousin Samira's **accounting job** is more at risk than mine.
A **robot milker** sale at the dairy show could change my hours.
do: Ask Uncle Karim **straight out** if he buys a robot milker.
**Wait** to see what neighbouring dairies do first.
feel: **Uneasy**, like a barn noise he decides is **the cat**.
S1.quote: My uncle could get talked into a robot milker by the salesman at the dairy show, and those machines cost the price of a house.
fieldNote: He places the risk **elsewhere first**, in offices and with his cousin.
He would rather **wait** than move first, in line with his caution.
The **barn noise** image shows quiet self-reassurance.

steps.text: Keep milking and saving on the same routine
Watch what the neighbouring dairies do before changing anything

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? That's mad. That's before the slurry store's paid off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I don't believe it until I see it. Then I'd go quiet. People round here don't like to talk about money or being scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it's true, my uncle's the type to sell. He's 61, and by 2031, when robots can milk and feed better than me, he'd be 66 and tired. The Dawson family next door would buy the land, put in machines, and I'd be a herdsman with no herd.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit my uncle down this winter and ask for the farm promise in writing, with a share of the herd. I'd save harder, stop the new truck I was going to buy, and get to six months. I don't really know what else, I'm not a computer person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, to be honest. I'd lose sleep over it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does it help that the robots come three years after the AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. The AI bit in 2028 takes Samira's books and Uncle's ordering, not my milking. So I get three more years in the parlour. But I'd spend those three years watching the clock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not a computer person. Would you change that if your job depended on it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to think about it. Part of me says yes, obviously. The other part says I'd be learning to run the thing that replaces me, and I'd still be 'surplus' in the end.

say: I'd say I **don't believe** it until I see it.
I'd then **go quiet**, as people here avoid money and fear talk.
think: Uncle Karim would likely **sell** at 66 once robots arrive in 2031.
The **Dawson family** would buy the land and machine it.
do: Ask Uncle Karim for the **farm promise in writing** this winter.
Cancel the **new truck** and reach six months of savings.
Hold back on **computer skills**, unsure if they'd help.
S2.quote: The Dawson family next door would buy the land, put in machines, and I'd be a herdsman with no herd.
fieldNote: The threat comes through his **uncle's choice to sell**, not directly.
The **three-year gap** feels like a countdown, not a chance.
He doubts **retraining** helps if he'd still be surplus.

steps.text: Ask Uncle Karim for the farm promise and a herd share in writing
Cancel the planned new truck purchase
Save hard to reach six months of bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Still quick, but you can see it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, let's see how it pans out. I wouldn't get worked up in front of people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me time to get things sorted with my uncle. Robots around 2034, I'm 35, he's 69. If the farm is in my name when the robots come, the robots work for me; if not, I'm out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the succession thing written up with a solicitor within a year, with Samira's help. I'd keep saving. And I'd keep milking, because if I'm going to take over, I need to be the one who knows the cows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but it's a job I can do something about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your uncle in that conversation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Uncle Karim I've given him eight years, and I need to know if I've got a future here. I'd say it at the kitchen table, not in the parlour, so he knows it's serious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if he says no?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd look for herdsman work on the bigger dairies near Wexley, while there's still some. I'd have a couple of years, maybe.

say: I'd say **let's see** how it pans out over a few years.
I'd **stay calm** in front of people and not get worked up.
think: Five years is time to settle **succession** with my uncle.
If the farm is **in my name** by 2034, robots work for me.
do: Get the succession written with a **solicitor** within a year.
Keep **saving** and keep running the herd.
Look for **herdsman work** near Wexley if his uncle says no.
feel: **Worried**, but it's a job he **can act on**.
S3.quote: If the farm is in my name when the robots come, the robots work for me; if not, I'm out.
fieldNote: Time turns his fear into a **family negotiation**.
He chooses the **kitchen table** for the serious talk.
He has a **fallback**: herdsman jobs on bigger dairies near Wexley.

steps.text: Get the farm succession written up with a solicitor within a year
Keep running the herd to stay the one who knows the cows
Look for herdsman jobs near Wexley if Uncle Karim says no

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a long time in farming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a lot can happen in ten years of dairy farming. Nobody knows what's coming with robots or milk prices or anything else, so I'd not pretend to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is enough for the farm to be mine, probably. Uncle Karim would be 71 by 2036 and ready to hand over. Then it's my choice whether to buy robots. I'd probably still be slow about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy a share of the herd from my uncle, maybe 20 cows over three years, using my savings. Keep milking. Watch what the bigger farms do with robots and only copy what works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared, just aware there's a lot I don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever use AI tools in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably once everyone else does. If the vet and the feed rep use them, I'll get dragged in. I just won't be first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep saying you'd be slow. Is that a choice or a worry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both. I know being slow costs money sometimes. But I've seen farmers go broke being first, and I've never seen one go broke being second.

say: I'd say **nobody knows** what ten years will bring to dairy farming.
I'd refuse to **pretend** I can predict robots, milk prices or anything else.
think: The farm would **probably be mine** by the time Uncle Karim is 71.
Buying robots would be **my choice**, and I'd still be slow.
do: Buy **20 cows** from his uncle over three years from savings.
Keep milking and **copy only** what works on bigger farms.
feel: **Uneasy**, aware of how much he **doesn't know**.
S4.quote: I've seen farmers go broke being first, and I've never seen one go broke being second.
fieldNote: A decade lets **succession** happen naturally before robots.
His **caution** is a deliberate strategy, not only fear.
He'll adopt AI only when the **vet and feed rep** do.

steps.text: Buy 20 cows from Uncle Karim over three years
Keep milking twice a day at Hillcrest
Copy robot use only after bigger farms prove it works

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my uncle would sell before I'm ready. What would help is something that makes it easier for old farmers to pass the farm to young ones, like tax breaks or help with solicitors.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the family side. On a family farm, a robot isn't the scary part; the scary part is a family deciding they'd rather have the money.

headlineQuote: On a family farm, a robot isn't the scary part; the scary part is a family deciding they'd rather have the money.
portrait: Yusuf is a 27-year-old **herdsman** on his uncle's 110-cow dairy farm.
His future rests on an **unwritten promise** that the farm will be his.
He **never uses AI** and prefers to be second rather than first.
He becomes **alarmed** at AGI by 2028, fearing his uncle sells to the Dawsons.
More warning turns his worry into a **succession** plan he can act on.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because Uncle Karim might sell before Yusuf is ready.
whatWouldHelp: **Tax breaks** or legal help so old farmers can pass farms to young ones.
